*(AI-generated comment)*

Regarding this comment (and the similar ones on `pthread_spin_trylock.c`, `pthread_spin_unlock.c`, and `pthread_once.c` about casting `int *` to `_Atomic int *`):

1. **This cast was already happening prior to this PR:** Previously, `a_cas`, `a_swap`, `a_store`, etc. in `atomic_arch.h` took `volatile int *p` and internally cast it to `(_Atomic int *)p` before calling `__c11_atomic_*`. All this PR did for those calls was move that same cast out of `atomic_arch.h` to the few remaining call sites where the public POSIX type (`pthread_once_t`, `pthread_spinlock_t`) is a plain `int`.
2. **The `*(volatile int *)` reads this replaces were actual C11 data races:** In `pthread_spin_lock.c` and `pthread_once.c`, `*(volatile int *)s` and `*(volatile int *)control == 2` were non-atomic `volatile` loads racing with atomic writes on other threads (emitting plain `i32.load` instead of `i32.atomic.load` in Wasm). Changing those to `*(_Atomic int *)` fixes the data race.
3. **Safe for target-specific libc code:** The C11 restriction against aliasing `T` and `_Atomic T` exists only because an implementation is permitted to give `_Atomic T` a different size, alignment, or representation than `T`. On Wasm/Clang, `int` and `_Atomic int` have identical size (`4`), alignment (`4`), and representation, and `__c11_atomic_*((_Atomic int *)p, ...)` lowers to the exact same LLVM IR as `__atomic_*((int *)p, ...)`.

This review comment is describing the old musl 1.1.x implementation rather than the current code:

- **In musl 1.1.x (prior to #13006):** `__get_locale` had its own internal `static int lock[2]` and did a lock-free fast-path walk over `loc_head` before acquiring `LOCK(lock)` and walking `loc_head` a second time.

issue.title: [lld][WebAssembly] Only report import attribute mismatches for undefined symbols
issue.body:
Previously, `updateExistingUndefined` immediately reported an error if two undefined references to a symbol had conflicting `import_module` or `import_name` attributes, even if the symbol was later resolved by a definition in another input file or LTO object.

This made `wasm-ld` dependent on input file ordering (succeeding when the definition appeared before the undefined references, but failing when it appeared after) and broke ThinLTO links where cross-module inlining synthesized a declaration with the default `env` import module for a symbol defined in bitcode.

Defer reporting import attribute mismatches until all input files and LTO objects have been processed, and only emit the error if the symbol remains undefined.

Fixes: https://github.com/emscripten-core/emscripten/issues/27939

issue.title: [libc] Replace `volatile` atomic locations in musl with `_Atomic`
issue.body:
Musl historically used `volatile` for atomic memory locations, lock variables, and synchronization struct members (`pthread_mutex_t`, `mtx_t`, `pthread_cond_t`, `cnd_t`, `pthread_rwlock_t`, `pthread_barrier_t`, `pthread_attr_t`, `sem_t`, `FILE::lock`, `libc.need_locks`, and `struct pthread` fields).

Replace these `volatile` uses with C11 `_Atomic` (and remove `volatile` from the thread-local `robust_list` / `__p` pointers in `pthread_mutex_t` and `struct pthread`, which are only `volatile` in upstream Linux musl for `SYS_set_robust_list` kernel inspection on process crash).

This has several benefits:
- Public synchronization types (`pthread_mutex_t`, `pthread_cond_t`, etc.) no longer have `volatile` union members, so Clang's `RecordDecl::hasVolatileMember()` is `false`. Compound-literal struct initializations in `em_task_queue.c` and `proxying.c` no longer emit stack temporaries and `volatile` `llvm.memcpy` calls (saving 292 bytes in `test_codesize_minimal_pthreads`).
- In single-threaded builds, LLVM lowers `_Atomic` accesses to plain non-volatile loads and stores that can be optimized away.
- In multi-threaded builds, direct reads of atomic fields emit proper atomic loads instead of non-atomic `volatile` loads.

Depends on #28211 and #28217

comment.body:
> It looks like this is a divergence from upstream musl? Do we know why they aren't doing this?

Gemini found a much better/details reasoning of why upstream musl used `volatile` instead of `_Atomic`:

Rich Felker introduced `volatile` across all atomic locations in upstream musl
commit [`56fbaa3bbe73`][musl-commit] (*"make all objects used with atomic
operations volatile"*, March 2015). From his commit message:

> *"...objects that may be modified by atomics are modeled as volatile, and the
> atomic operations performed on them by other threads are modeled as
> asynchronous stores by hardware which happens to be acting on the request of
> another thread. ... this all seems less than ideal, but it's the best we can
> do without mandating a C11 compiler and using the C11 model for atomics."*

In Emscripten, we only use Clang, which supports `_Atomic` in all C and C++
language modes as a builtin keyword.

[musl-commit]: https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=56fbaa3bbe73f12af2bfbbcf2adb196e6f9fe264

issue.title: [pthreads] Avoid compound literal assignment for structs with volatile members
issue.body:
In C, assigning a compound literal through a pointer (`*ptr = (T){...}`) constructs a temporary object on the stack and copies it to `*ptr`. For plain structs, LLVM's SROA and `MemCpyOpt` passes eliminate the stack temporary and initialize `*ptr` in place.

However, when `T` contains an `_Atomic` field or a `volatile` member (including musl's `pthread_mutex_t` and `pthread_cond_t`, whose internal unions contain `volatile` members, even inside an inactive union branch), Clang emits the aggregate copy as a `volatile` `llvm.memcpy`. Because the copy is marked `volatile`, LLVM cannot elide the stack temporary and must allocate stack space, initialize the temporary on the stack, and `volatile`-copy every field (and any struct padding) into `*ptr`.

Avoid this overhead in `em_task_queue.c` and `proxying.c` by:
- Using `memset` followed by explicit field stores for heap-allocated structs (`em_task_queue_create`, `em_proxying_queue_create`, and `em_proxying_ctx_init_callback`).
- Initializing stack-allocated `em_proxying_ctx` directly at declaration in `emscripten_proxy_sync_with_ctx` (`T ctx = {...}`), which initializes `ctx` in place without a temporary or `volatile` copy.

issue.title: [js-compiler] Optimize `getTransitiveDeps` and `isDecorator`
issue.body:
Since #28144, every C define in `struct_info.json` is added to
`LibraryManager.library` as three entries (`$FOO`, `$FOO__const`, and
`$FOO__internal`). Adding hundreds more constants to `struct_info.json`
(as in #28199) would otherwise incur two compile-time performance costs
in `compiler.mjs`:

1. When #28054 first proposed memoizing `getTransitiveDeps`, `__deps`
   only contained explicitly declared dependencies (~39k node visits).
   Since #28052 (automatic JS library dependency scanning) and
   #27981 / #28144 (exposing `struct_info.json` C defines as `__const`
   JS library symbols), every referenced helper and constant is recorded
   in `__deps`. With hundreds more constants added in #28199, uncached
   node visits in `--symbols-only` mode grow to ~56k on default builds
   and 165k-250k+ with GL/GLFW (~25-90 ms). Memoizing
   `getTransitiveDeps` in `transitiveDepsCache` (`src/jsifier.mjs`)
   avoids re-walking shared dependency subgraphs, keeping visits to
   ~11k-13k and cutting the pass to ~18 ms with GL/GLFW.

2. Each `struct_info.json` constant adds three keys to
   `LibraryManager.library`, which is iterated over in multiple passes
   that call `isDecorator` (`src/utility.mjs`) on every key. Using
   `lastIndexOf('__')` and a `Set` lookup instead of
   `decoratorSuffixes.some` with `endsWith` avoids scanning all 15
   decorator suffixes for every key in the library.

See: #28054, #28199

issue.title: Direct `eval()` in JS libraries disables Terser `reduce_vars` and `unused` across the entire file
issue.body:
In #27949 and #27987, we enabled `reduce_vars: true`, `unused: true`, and
`toplevel: true` in the Terser `compress` pass in `tools/acorn-optimizer.mjs`.
This is what inlines top-level `const` declarations (including all C defines
from `cDefs`) into their use sites and removes the `const` declarations in
optimized non-Closure builds.

However, whenever any function included in the build contains a direct `eval()`
call, Terser marks that function's scope and **every enclosing ancestor scope**
(up to `AST_Toplevel`, or the `MODULARIZE` factory function) with
`uses_eval = true`. When `uses_eval` is set on a scope, Terser completely
disables both `reduce_vars` and `unused` for all declarations in that scope.

### Minimal reproduction

```js
const ENOENT = 44;
const EINVAL = 28;
function foo(x) { return x === ENOENT ? EINVAL : 0; }
function run_script(s) { eval(s); }
globalThis.keep(foo, run_script);
```

Running Terser with Emscripten's `compress` settings produces:

```js
const ENOENT=44;const EINVAL=28;function foo(x){return x===ENOENT?EINVAL:0}function run_script(s){eval(s)}globalThis.keep(foo,run_script);
```

Because `run_script` calls `eval(s)`, `ENOENT` and `EINVAL` are neither inlined
into `foo` nor removed from the top-level output.

### Affected library code

Any build that pulls in one of the following gets no top-level `const` inlining
or Terser dead-variable elimination:

1. `emscripten_run_script`, `emscripten_run_script_int`, and
   `emscripten_run_script_string` in `src/lib/libcore.js` (also included in any
   `-sINCLUDE_FULL_LIBRARY` build)
2. `$addEmAsm` and `$addEmJs` in `src/lib/libdylink.js` (included in
   `-sMAIN_MODULE` / dynamic linking builds)
3. `emscripten_async_wget_script` in `src/lib/libbrowser.js` (when
   `ENVIRONMENT_MAY_BE_NODE` is active)
4. `-sWASM=2` fallback loader in `src/shell.js` and `src/shell_minimal.js`

### Possible solutions

1. **Switch to indirect `(0, eval)(...)` or `eval?.(...)` where appropriate:**
   Indirect `eval` executes in global scope and does not cause Terser to mark
   enclosing scopes with `uses_eval`. Caveat: under `-sMODULARIZE` or
   `-sEXPORT_ES6`, indirect `eval` cannot see module-scoped internal symbols
   (such as `Module`, `HEAP8`, `UTF8ToString`), which `$addEmAsm`/`$addEmJs` or
   some `emscripten_run_script` callers may rely on.
2. **Inline `const` primitives in `tools/acorn-optimizer.mjs` (or mask `eval`
   during `minify_sync`):**
   Emscripten's own `JSDCE` pass already ignores dynamic `eval` scope effects
   (and `src/jsifier.mjs` explicitly compensates for `eval(` by conservatively
   adding `$HEAP*` dependencies). Masking direct `eval` from Terser (or
   inlining top-level primitive `const` declarations in `acorn-optimizer.mjs`)
   would preserve direct `eval` scoping at runtime while allowing Terser to
   optimize the rest of the module.

issue.title: [pthreads] Avoid compound literal assignment for structs with volatile members
issue.body:
In C, assigning a compound literal through a pointer (`*ptr = (T){...}`) constructs a temporary object on the stack and copies it to `*ptr`. For plain structs, LLVM's SROA and `MemCpyOpt` passes eliminate the stack temporary and initialize `*ptr` in place.

However, when `T` contains an `_Atomic` field or a `volatile` member (including musl's `pthread_mutex_t` and `pthread_cond_t`, whose internal unions contain `volatile` members, even inside an inactive union branch), Clang emits the aggregate copy as a `volatile` `llvm.memcpy`. Because the copy is marked `volatile`, LLVM cannot elide the stack temporary and must allocate stack space, initialize the temporary on the stack, and `volatile`-copy every field (and any struct padding) into `*ptr`.

Avoid this overhead in `em_task_queue.c` and `proxying.c` by:
- Using `memset` followed by explicit field stores for heap-allocated structs (`em_task_queue_create`, `em_proxying_queue_create`, and `em_proxying_ctx_init_callback`).
- Initializing stack-allocated `em_proxying_ctx` directly at declaration in `emscripten_proxy_sync_with_ctx` (`T ctx = {...}`), which initializes `ctx` in place without a temporary or `volatile` copy.

issue.title: acosh() returns finite values for some negative arguments (backport musl "math: fix acosh for x<0")
issue.body:
### Environment

- emscripten main (4264ab9): `system/lib/libc/musl/src/math/acosh.c` still has the pre-fix musl code
- Seen through quickjs-emscripten 0.32.0 (QuickJS compiled with emscripten), where `Math.acosh(-49152)` is `-3.7534177368329567`
- Checked on 2026-11-03

### Reproduction

```c
#include <math.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    volatile double a = -0x1.8p15, b = -51274.919509887695, c = -6.7e7;
    printf("%g %g %g\n", acosh(a), acosh(b), acosh(c));
    return 0;
}
```

- Expected: `nan nan nan`
- Actual, with the current musl code: `-3.75342 -4.28713 12.291`

### Cause

The old musl `acosh` drops the sign bit when it classifies the argument (`unsigned e = u.i >> 52 & 0x7ff;`), so some
x ≤ −2 go through the `log(2*x - 1/(x+sqrt(x*x-1)))` branch and return a finite value.

Fixed upstream in musl
[3e80328d](https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=3e80328d45b73604012b9b174f11e3ed632005ce)
("math: fix acosh for x<0", 2026-08-03): keep the sign bit (`unsigned e = u.i >> 52;`) and return `(x-x)/(x-x)` when
`e & 0x800`. It is a 7+/6− change to that one file and applies to emscripten's copy unchanged. I compiled the old and the
new function body natively against glibc's libm: the old body gives the values above, and the new one returns NaN for
every x < 1 and matches glibc for x ≥ 1. I have not built emscripten's libc with the change.

### Impact

`Math.acosh` in JavaScript engines compiled with emscripten returns these values, although ECMA-262 requires NaN for any
argument below 1 ([Math.acosh](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-math.acosh), step 4).

### Related

- The same old code is in WebAssembly/wasi-libc; reported there separately.

Same issue reported to wasi-libc: WebAssembly/wasi-libc#901
